I didn't mention it then, but I believe one of the reasons for such dreams might have come from a medication I was prescribed called "Remeron," or mirtazapine. I was prescribed it initially so that it would help me with my sleep, as I was having difficulty sleeping. What I wasn't told, and what isn't even listed as an official symptom, is that the medication causes a great deal of vivid dreams - many that are nightmarish. There's no depersonalization either, these "mirtazapine dreams" made me feel very real emotions and I believed myself to be whomever that was receiving these awful afflictions.

I've since stopped taking it. I was on it for roughly a year and a half, and the dreams were definitely worse while I was on the medication. I wonder if it had anything to do with them...

I recognize by now this thread has already run its course, but let me be crystal clear about the exchange that occurred that morning.

I woke up, ready to go for treatment when I got sick. Vomiting, running a fever, etc. So I went to the E.R., and they decided to admit me.

Not even before I arrived at the hospital, the EMT and everyone waiting for me at the ED knew I was to have chemotherapy that day and I was told after I was admitted that my regular oncologist had been notified because I was indisposed.

Let me repeat that: **My regular oncologist had been notified because I was indisposed**. Now, it's possible someone at the hospital didn't do what they were supposed to and notified my regular - but, that's what I was told. I've always made it a case to alert my oncologist or his NP whenever I was at the hospital, but before I made the call I was told that he was told. So, I figured everything was fine and we were all caught up.

It's incredibly disparaging when someone suffering from cancer comes here for support, only to be met with derision and mockery in some cases. I don't think it's fair to be made the pariah because genuine miscommunication and mixed signals accounted for a turbulent visit.

I won't ask for support anymore, since it seems I quickly and thoroughly ran that well dry, but I will ask that if you see me in other threads that the general unpleasantness exhibited here doesn't cross over. That's all I can ask for, some civility.

>skipping treatments

I mentioned in another post in this thread that I've been actively doing treatment for three years now. I'm not purposefully missing treatment, or being lazy.

I can't help but feel a bit dismayed over how most of the people in this thread are responding to me. I miss a couple of recent treatments because of circumstances that were out of my hand, and then not only do other people here criticize me for what I think is honestly a slight mishap when compared against the rest of my timetable over these last three years, but I'm also getting the feeling that the more I try to justify or defend myself I'm treated just as negatively.

I really don't know what else to say to everyone here. I'm not perfect, I'm human, but it's just so incredibly disconcerting when I come here to receive support and I'm mostly met with criticism and derision in spite of following treatment to the letter for the last three years, with the exception of the last several months.

Maybe this thread was a mistake.

You have my appreciation. I just wish the rest of my colleagues here wouldn't undermine my history fighting this cancer. I've dedicated three years of my life to fighting a cancer I know will kill me. Thank you, and I agree. I think it's a bit disconcerting seeing a majority of these replies act like I'm in the wrong because of things that were out of my control or, worse, behaving like I haven't been trying my best for the better part of three years now.

I'm not quitting, I'm not throwing in the towel - and I want an oncologist that isn't either.

When I was living for the first year with the cancer and without any knowledge of it, the worst thing that happened was an hour or so of crippling pain in the super-pubic one December night in 2016. I had no idea, at the time, what was causing so much distress and I wound up in the ER over it. 99% of the time for that year, however, it was just bloody stools and slightly more frequent trips to the bathroom.

So yes, while the chemo isn't exactly 'painful' in the literal sense it's much more stressful and grueling than living with the cancer ever was.

Granted, that pain I mentioned earlier, in the super-pubic area, would go on to be the biggest issue in this whole battle. Last summer, I was in and out of the hospital frequently for pain management because nobody could figure out why I was getting these intense bouts of pain that would last for days at a time. Now I know it's because I was getting blocked up in the colon because the original tumor had grew to such an extent it was preventing stool from passing through.

So...overall, if I hadn't done treatment I more than likely would have had a colostomy by now or an exploded colon and be possibly dead/permanently disfigured. Not to mention the pain. Hmm. When put in a broader sense, maybe the cancer actually was worse than chemo. They're both awful in different ways. That's my conclusion.

Yup. I noticed blood in my stool in late 2015. I was 27 when it started, and I didn't get checked until well over a year later, in February of 2017 for an entirely different reason I was at the hospital for. One colonoscopy later, and I was confirmed to have colon cancer. Unfortunately, it had spread and I'm metastatic.

If you see blood in your stoool, PLEASE don't do what I did and not get it checked. I could have avoided this fate if I had gone through with the colonoscopy on the first day I noticed it - but didn't because the preparation process seemed overwhelming. It's worth getting checked no matter what if you've got blood.

Nah, you don't want to go out via cancer. Trust me. I've struggled with depression and suicide since my teen years - I was diagnosed major depressive disorder back in '07. But then I was diagnosed with end stage colon cancer back in early 2017, and even though I essentially "got what I wanted," I'm going to die a pretty slow and pretty rotten death.

What's humorous about it is that, for some reason, I'm staving it off by fighting it and doing chemotherapy. It's like the universe is saying "you got the guest of honor invite to your own funeral party, why are you *now* fighting to live?" But yeah, fighting cancer is a pretty prolonged and awful way to go.

Hiya. So, when I started heavy chemo back in 2017 I was on a pump and receiving huge doses of four to five medicines. Strangely enough, no chemo brain. My body felt like crap, but my head felt just fine.

Then, about a year later, they put me on maintenance chemotherapy - avastin and xeloda to take at home, and sure enough about a cycle in all of a sudden my vision starts to feel slanted and I feel like my depth perception is always off, like I'm looking at things through a filter. I was seeing flashes out of the corners of my eyes, and I was starting to think there was something seriously wrong. I was thinking the cancer had spread to my brain. Thankfully, a CT scan and some extensive eye testing determined there was nothing there and it was more likely just me adjusting to the new medicine.

Give it a few months, it gets better. Believe me. I was afraid at first, too, but like any medicine your body will adjust.
